# Introduction

The **Unraveling TTRPG** is a tabletop role-playing game designed to bring the rich, dark fantasy universe of *The Unraveling* series to the gaming table. Drawing on the full body of the source material – from the HALO system’s unique dice mechanics to the *Threshold/Wolfspace* cosmology and the mythic *First Flame* creation story – this game blends **epic weak-to-strong character progression** with **story-driven, cosmic adventure**【2†L9-L17】. Players will begin as mortals in a modern dark-fantasy world and can rise to influence – or even become – the divine powers that shape reality. The design emphasizes **intuitive yet deep mechanics**, **narrative immersion**, and a flexible, **modular framework** to accommodate homebrew expansions and alternate settings. All core systems and lore are tightly integrated with the established universe’s tone and themes, ensuring the game feels authentic to the world of *The Unraveling* while remaining accessible to new players.

## Design Goals and Philosophy

The development of this TTRPG is guided by six core design principles. These principles ensure the game captures the spirit of the source material and provides a satisfying experience that balances complexity with clarity:

- **Intuitive Complexity:** *Depth through simple building blocks.* The system should allow emergent gameplay and intricate mechanical interactions to arise from a relatively simple base rule-set. Patterns and mechanics will be easy to learn, but **combine in creative ways** to yield rich possibilities. For example, players will **mix a few core elements (attributes, dice outcomes, narrative tags)** to generate complex effects, rather than juggle dozens of exceptions. This “easy to learn, hard to master” approach means that even newcomers can grasp the basics, while veterans find **new synergies** over time. The goal is to hide complexity *within* intuitive patterns – much like the HALO oracle’s layered interpretation system provides a logical flow for even complex spreads【17†L123-L127】. Players can **focus on story and strategy** instead of rote calculation.

- **Narrative-Driven Play:** *Story and character above all.* Every mechanic is designed to support storytelling, character development, and emotional immersion. Dice rolls and stats will never overshadow the narrative; instead they **amplify dramatic moments**. Character arcs and relationships have mechanical weight – for instance, a character confronting their *Shadow* (inner fears) in the Reflection realm might gain bonuses for meaningful roleplay. The game encourages cinematic descriptions and **visceral outcomes** in line with the source material’s tone (e.g. when Lilith fights in the novels, “**bones break… reality screams… she pukes up starlight**” – the supernatural feels personal and intense【14†L221-L229】). By tying progression to story milestones (in the novels, each arc corresponded to mastering a new realm【2†L23-L30】), the system ensures that **mechanical growth follows narrative fulfillment**, reinforcing the feeling of a living story. GMs are provided tools like **oracle dice prompts, fate scripts, and character motivation frameworks** to facilitate collaborative story creation. Ultimately, the rules serve to **heighten the drama** – from cosmic battles to intimate character moments – not to drown it out.

- **Modular Architecture:** *A flexible core with plug-in options.* The game’s rule architecture is modular, allowing groups and third-party creators to add or swap content without breaking the system’s balance. The **core mechanics are self-contained** and define clear boundaries (for attributes, difficulty scales, damage ranges, etc.), so new modules (e.g. a cyberpunk setting, an alternate magic school, or a custom realm) can slot in by adhering to those standards. This modular design is inspired by the HALO engine’s table-agnostic philosophy – the oracle’s core tables can be **“swapped as your mythology evolves”**【17†L36-L43】 – and by the idea of expandable content packs in the HALO board game prototype【15†L1-L4】. In practice, this means the TTRPG will support *expansions and homebrew*: new Realm guides, bestiaries, or rule add-ons can be created as “plug-ins.” For example, a creator might publish an expansion with an **alternate cosmology or additional Biomes**, or a **culture-specific pantheon**; as long as they follow the core’s scaling guidelines, the expansion will integrate seamlessly. House rules can be enabled or disabled like modules (e.g. a *gritty realism* module for harsher wounds, or a *fate cinematic* module for more narrative control). This ensures the system can **grow with its community**, and groups can tailor the experience to their preferred playstyle without unraveling the foundational balance.

- **Divinity and Apotheosis:** *Mortal to divine progression.* One of the most distinctive aspects of the game is the **path to godhood**. The design includes systems that let player characters gradually ascend to divine status, taking on roles akin to the *Thrones* in the lore. Just as the lore describes the Thrones as beings positioned at cosmological “**compactification nodes**” feeding on soul flows【10†L13-L21】【10†L63-L70】, high-level characters in the game can challenge these positions or even claim them. The rules for **apotheosis** involve epic quests and profound transformations: characters cultivate enough Quintessence (cosmic energy) or fulfill grand narrative conditions to undergo **Ascension**. Upon ascending, a character can establish a **divine realm or pocket dimension** of their own, gain a title (akin to becoming a new Throne or lesser god), and mechanically gain *domain powers*. These powers allow them to **influence cosmological structures** – for example, altering the cycle of reincarnation or creating new “compactification nodes” (echoing the scholarly speculation that **“new nodes could be created through sufficient local quintessential density”**【10†L156-L164】). Crucially, ascending doesn’t end the game; it shifts it into a new phase of play where **the challenges become cosmic** (managing a realm, contending with other deities, preventing reality from fracturing under one’s influence, etc.). Worship, faith, and followers become tangible resources, detailed below. Despite the lofty scale, the design will keep gameplay intuitive at the divine level by extending the same core mechanics (for example, domain actions might still be resolved with HALO dice rolls, just at a grand scale). This principle ensures that **becoming a god is a playable outcome**, not just a narrative epilogue – a natural extension of the progression fantasy built into the universe【14†L119-L121】.

- **Integration of Core Lore:** *Mechanics reflect mythology.* The **established universe lore is directly woven into the rules**, so that playing the game feels like inhabiting the novels’ world. Rather than abstract or generic fantasy tropes, we use the specific concepts from the Unraveling series as the basis for game systems. For example, the eight cosmic layers of reality – the **Eight Biomes/Realms** from *The Unraveling* – form the game’s fundamental setting structure, each with its unique properties and gameplay (detailed later)【14†L125-L133】. The cosmic war between the **Pattern (structure of reality) and the Hollow (entropy)** provides not just backstory but a driving force for campaign conflicts, with mechanical representation: e.g. corruption by the Hollow is a risk characters face, and **Hollow manifestations** form a category of adversaries【14†L147-L155】. The *First Flame mythos* (the creation of the world by the First Flame out of loneliness, the role of the Firstborn, and the erased Mother Goddess) is reflected in the cosmology and divine magic of the game – clerics or ascended PCs might literally channel the “First Flame” or invoke Lilith’s lost name, and the tension between the Father (order) and Mother (chaos) aspects can influence miracles【8†L29-L37】【8†L43-L47】. Even smaller lore elements find mechanical hooks: the **Roads Between** maintained by Solomon in the Threshold realm – where travelers pay memories as toll【2†L155-L160】 – is realized as a travel mechanic; the **Keystone words** that compress reality-manipulation commands【2†L139-L147】 could be a system of one-word spells; the mysterious Watcher faction becomes a patron option, etc. By aligning rules with lore (for instance, using the five Aspects of Quintessence – Memory, Passion, Reason, Will, Essence – as possible character attributes【1†L81-L89】, or modeling *Wolfspace* pocket dimensions as adventuring zones), the game achieves a cohesive feel. Players who know the books will find **familiar terms and concepts at every turn**, and those new to the world will organically learn its lore through gameplay. This principle addresses a key goal from the author’s notes: the mythology should **“BE the HALO system, not just echo it,”** embedding the unique metaphysics into the game’s DNA【8†L13-L17】.

- **HALO-Based Advancement:** *The HALO archetype dice as the core of growth and magic.* Character progression and abilities revolve around the **Hidden Axis Labyrinthine Oracle (HALO)** system of three dice and their archetypal qualities. Instead of traditional classes or a generic leveling system, a character’s identity and power are defined by the **HALO trinity**: **Flow, Mirror, Gate** – the three aspects of power represented by three dice【8†L79-L87】. As the character grows, they **“unlock”** these dice one by one and eventually in combination, mirroring the progression from novice to reality-warper. This concept is built directly on the source material’s power system: the novels explicitly describe Lily’s powers in terms of HALO dice outcomes (e.g. *“FLOW: SURGE. MIRROR: SHADOW. GATE: RELEASE.”* to channel a devastating attack【14†L243-L252】). The game mechanizes that process. Early on, a player might attune to one Aspect (say, Flow) based on their character’s approach to the world, giving them intuitive abilities related to momentum, energy, and change. As they advance, they gain the others (Mirror: perception/illusion, Gate: connections/transitions), eventually able to **“triple-cast”** and combine aspects for extraordinary effects. The **HALO dice themselves are used in gameplay** both as randomizers and as symbolic prompts – for instance, magic and superhuman feats are resolved by rolling or selecting HALO dice faces rather than, say, spell slots. The eight faces of each HALO die (with thematic concepts like *Surge, Shadow, Gate, etc.*) provide an *intuitive vocabulary* for players to describe and shape their powers. This ties character growth to an *oracle-like creativity*: players interpret their dice results in narrative terms (similar to how one would interpret a tarot draw), making each use of power a story beat, not just a number. By using HALO as the foundation for advancement and supernatural interaction, we ensure that the **mechanical progression is the narrative progression**. The character’s journey from *Spark* to *Crown* (detailed below) isn’t just a level grind – it’s an unfolding revelation of their **true archetype and destiny** within the cosmic order of The Unraveling【14†L115-L123】.

Each of these principles is expanded in the sections below, detailing how they manifest in specific subsystems of the TTRPG design.

## Core Mechanics Overview

**System Core:** The Unraveling TTRPG uses a **hybrid system** that blends traditional skill checks with narrative oracle elements. At its heart, characters are defined by a set of **Aspects** instead of mundane attributes like Strength or Intelligence. The primary Aspects are derived from the world’s cosmology and the HALO system, ensuring flavor and mechanics align. These include the **three HALO aspects** (Flow, Mirror, Gate) which govern supernatural feats and archetypal approaches to problems, as well as **fundamental Quintessence aspects** like Memory, Passion, Reason, Will, and Essence (drawn from the scholarly framework of quintessence that underpins reality【1†L81-L89】). In practical terms, an *Aspect* score represents a character’s capability in that domain – for example, a high *Passion* might aid emotional influence or fueling magic, while a strong *Will* helps resist domination or drive miracles, and a developed *Flow* aspect indicates the character excels at adapting to momentum and change.

**Task Resolution:** When characters attempt actions with uncertain outcomes, they roll dice against a difficulty. The core mechanic uses a **d100 or 2d10 system** for skill checks (percentile for granularity) combined with **narrative dice** from HALO for flavor. A typical check involves two steps: first, determine basic success via a percentile roll under a target (modified by Aspect levels, skills, and circumstances), then interpret a **HALO die** (or dice) to characterize the outcome. For instance, a player sneaking past a celestial sentinel might roll under their *Reason* Aspect + Stealth skill to succeed, then roll the **Mirror die** for narrative nuance – a result of *Shadow* could mean they remain unseen but stir something unseen within themselves, whereas *Witness* might reveal an observation they make during the attempt. In combat or dramatic confrontations, the game leans into **degrees of success and narrative beats**: exceeding a difficulty by a large margin or rolling a special percentile (like doubles) could “unlock” a HALO oracle roll that adds an unexpected benefit or complication. This merges the deterministic resolution (did you succeed, yes/no/how well) with a *story twist generator*. The HALO oracle tables from the source are repurposed for in-game use – GMs can use the **Axis/Vector/Consequence** tables【6†L39-L47】【6†L85-L93】 to quickly generate prompts for twists, encouraging emergent storytelling. 

**Character Abilities and Skills:** Characters have a **skill system** for mundane and specialized tasks (e.g. Athletics, Investigation, Technology, etc.), but even these are tied to the narrative Aspects rather than fixed physical stats. Each skill is linked to one or more Aspects, chosen flexibly depending on how the character approaches a task. For example, a character could attempt to solve an engineering puzzle by applying *Reason* (logic) or by applying *Mirror* (seeing the pattern) – the player describes the approach, and the GM assigns the appropriate Aspect for the roll. This encourages creative problem-solving and lets the fiction dictate the mechanic (supporting narrative-driven play). 

**Emergent Mechanics & Combos:** The core rules are designed to be **lightweight** on their own, but with many **combinatory hooks** that lead to emergent complexity. Rather than dozens of rigid subsystems, we have a few universal mechanics that **stack**. For example, **Tags** are a core concept: conditions or qualities (like “On Fire”, “Inspired by Ancestors”, “Gravity Warp”) that can attach to characters or scenes. These tags are simply descriptors with a rule effect (usually a small bonus, penalty, or trigger), but they interact: multiple tags can synergize or conflict in interesting ways, and players can leverage tags creatively (using a “Storm” tag on the environment to empower a *Flow: Surge* lightning attack, for instance). The **HALO dice combination system** (detailed under magic and progression) is another major source of emergent gameplay: by mixing different aspect effects, players can devise *new “moves” on the fly*. The core rules encourage GMs to say “Yes, and” to these combinations, using guidelines to adjudicate outcomes logically. Because each HALO facet has an intuitive meaning, even complex multi-step plans can be resolved by breaking them into **intuitive components**. This structure keeps things feeling **coherent and fair** – patterns in the rules mirror patterns in the narrative, making it easier for everyone to follow the cause and effect. In summary, the core mechanics emphasize **flexibility and intuition**: a unified resolution system, flavored by oracle dice, that can handle everything from hacking a computer to exorcising a demon, with the differences coming from *how the story is described* rather than entirely separate rule sets.

**Conflict and Challenges:** Conflict can be physical, social, or spiritual in this game, and all are handled with similar mechanics. Turn-based action scenes (combat or high-stakes encounters) use an **exchange-based system** rather than strict second-by-second rounds. In each exchange, everyone declares intentions and we determine outcome and order with contested Aspect rolls. Damage and consequences are tracked through a mix of **Health** (for physical integrity) and **Ego** or **Quintessence** (for mental/spiritual strain). For example, facing a terrifying Hollow apparition might deal *Ego damage* (sapping Will or Passion) instead of physical harm. Characters can mitigate harm with **Aegis** – a resource akin to luck or divine favor, which players can spend to avoid catastrophic failure. (Notably, **Aegis tokens** appear in the HALO board game as a protection mechanic【17†L129-L133】, and here they serve a similar role to keep heroes alive for the big moments.) By unifying the approach to all conflict types and giving players tools to avoid an unlucky death (at the cost of scarce resources), the system ensures dramatic encounters are dangerous but encourage heroic risk-taking and story continuity.

Overall, the core mechanics establish a **balanced foundation**: numerical where needed for fairness, but always **interpreted through the lens of the story**. This creates a play experience where **rolling the dice moves the story forward**, uncovering new facets of the narrative in the process.

## Progression and Cultivation System (HALO-Based)

The progression system is directly inspired by cultivation fantasy tropes and the HALO power hierarchy from the source material. Characters advance through **distinct tiers of enlightenment/power**, each tier unlocking new abilities, scope, and narrative significance. These tiers, called **Cultivation Levels**, are modeled after the stages mentioned in the Unraveling notes【14†L114-L121】:

- **Spark-Touched** – the character is **barely awakened** to the supernatural, just beginning to feel the currents of quintessence around them【14†L115-L121】. At this entry tier, a character might have *one* minor ability or a faint HALO resonance (e.g. occasional prophetic dreams or a knack for small coincidences). Mechanics: the player gains a **Halo Spark** – a once-per-session intuition or lucky break reflecting nascent power. Attributes and skills are mostly human-normal, but the character becomes aware that greater forces exist.

- **Flame-Kindled** – the character **ignites their inner flame**, fully awakening to the HALO system with **one die (aspect) active**【14†L115-L121】. They choose one HALO Aspect (Flow, Mirror, or Gate) as their primary *Archetype*, which defines their early style. For example, a **Flow-Kindled** hero can manipulate kinetic energy or emotions in motion; a **Mirror-Kindled** one perceives truths and alters perceptions; a **Gate-Kindled** one opens portals or binds oaths. Mechanics: the character gains a **suite of basic powers** related to their chosen die (e.g. a small list of tier-1 techniques or spells). They can roll their one active HALO die for magical actions, while the other two aspects remain dormant (perhaps accessible only via story artifacts or intense effort). This stage corresponds to a low-level adventurer who has just stepped into the supernatural world.

- **Triple-Cast** – at this stage, the character has **awakened all three HALO dice** and can use Flow, Mirror, and Gate in concert【14†L115-L121】. This is a **major milestone** akin to completing the early arcs of the novel where Lily fully embraces her power. Mechanics: the character can **“roll fate”** by casting all three dice together or in sequence. In gameplay, this might mean they can create custom effects by selecting one result from each HALO category to describe a miraculous outcome. For example, combining *Bloom* (Flow) + *Name* (Mirror) + *Key* (Gate) could let them create a new lifeform keyed to a true name; combining *Surge* + *Pattern* + *Gate* might let them break a minor rule of reality temporarily. These combinations encourage **emergent spellcasting** – players essentially craft their own powers using the HALO lexicon, making magic very free-form yet bounded by the conceptual limits of those words. At Triple-Cast, characters also start to significantly outclass ordinary foes; they stand as mid-tier “superhumans” able to take on small armies or lesser demons.

- **Axis-Walker** – named after the “Axis” of the HALO (and literally walking the Axes of reality), this tier grants the character **the ability to traverse between realms/biomes**【14†L117-L120】. They can **move through the Threshold** and other layers at will, no longer bound to the Fundament (physical world). Narrative-wise, this is when adventures become interdimensional – characters might literally walk into the Labyrinth realm to alter probabilities or step into the Web to seek information from the collective unconscious. Mechanics: Axis-Walkers gain **Realm Access** as an ability. They learn the secret of **Corner Transit** – slipping around the edges of reality as described in Wolfspace theory【1†L21-L25】 – allowing them to find or create portals. In gameplay, this might involve making a roll against a realm’s entry difficulty and paying some cost (e.g. a memory for Threshold passage, as per the lore’s Roads Between toll【2†L155-L160】). Combat/ability-wise, being an Axis-Walker also means they can incorporate realm effects: for example, pulling a foe partially into the Labyrinth to confuse them. Essentially, the **cosmology fully opens up** at this stage. Axis-Walkers can also start accumulating **followers or fame** on a larger scale due to their legendary exploits.

- **Labyrinth-Weaver** – at this high tier, a character can **reshape the “maze” of reality** itself【14†L117-L120】. The title implies mastery over the *Labyrinth realm* (realm of probability and choice) and by extension, influence over fate, causality, and even narrative outcomes. Mechanics: A Labyrinth-Weaver gains the ability to perform **reality edits** on a small scale – for example, retroactively declaring they “prepared” something or tweaking a recent event (a nod to the toroidal timeline concept where time loops back【14†L288-L296】). They might spend a resource (like *Clarity* or *Quintessence points*) to alter a detail of a scene, with GM mediation. This is the tier where **cause and effect become malleable** in the character’s hands: e.g. they can ensure one specific possible outcome in a complex situation comes true (within reason). In story terms, Labyrinth-Weavers are the ones who **“cheat” destiny** or set up gambits that pay off arcs later. On the HALO dice side, this might allow **advanced combos** – perhaps picking two results from one die or influencing die outcomes (like “locking” one die face in place for a roll). They could also create **minor pocket dimensions** or alternate routes in Wolfspace, effectively changing the dungeon (or Labyrinth) layout of reality. At this point, characters operate on par with demigods or the most powerful immortal beings in the setting, barring the Thrones.

- **Oracle** – this penultimate tier marks a character who can **see the flow of time and possibility clearly**【14†L119-L121】. They are called “Oracle” because they have one foot in the Sight realm (pure perception) and one in the Engine (the underlying code of reality). Mechanics: Oracles gain **precognition and omniscience abilities** in limited form. For example, an Oracle can declare “I have foreseen this” to gain insight or a reroll; they can ask the GM meta-questions about the plot (“what will happen if we do X?”) reflecting their character’s transcendent knowledge. The toroidal timeline concept becomes a toy in their hands – they might sense echoes from past or future loops, or send messages to themselves through time. In combat or challenges, an [redacted:third-party-name] can perform feats like **parallel processing** (taking multiple actions by exploring different timeline branches) or **absolute defense** (avoiding an attack because in a million timelines it missed). The game will cap and structure these powers to avoid analysis paralysis (perhaps using a point system or one oracle action per session rule), but the idea is that *the character has effectively surpassed normal linear causality*. They also become major figures in the world, able to influence **cosmic-scale politics**; NPC angels, demons, or factions may defer to or fear them. Essentially, by the Oracle stage the characters are the equals of the setting’s most legendary figures (ancient Keepers, Watchers【2†L125-L129】, etc.), save for the creator or the Thrones.

- **Crown (Ascendant)** – the final tier of mortal advancement is reaching the **Crown**, meaning transcendence and nascent godhood【14†L119-L121】. This level is named after the Crown realm (the highest realm of transcendence) and signifies that the character is “**approaching the Infinite, memories of godhood bleeding through**”【14†L119-L121】. In the story, the Crown is the ultimate state; in the game, achieving the Crown tier means the character is effectively a Lesser Deity or about to become a full deity. Mechanics: Upon hitting Crown, a character undergoes an **Apotheosis event** (detailed in the next section on divinity) – they might claim a Throne if one is available or even create a new one if circumstances allow【10†L156-L164】【10†L169-L172】. They gain a **Divine Domain** (an area of influence like “Fire” or “Memory” or “Freedom”) which grants them powers potentially affecting entire regions or populations. In play, Crown-tier characters can literally **change the rules of the game** in their domain: for example, a Crown of War could declare that no violence may occur in their presence unless they permit it. They also begin to recall the **primordial memory** of the First Flame (or whatever cosmic source suits the campaign’s mythos): this could manifest as guidance from the Creator or fragments of understanding about the true nature of reality. The Crown tier is meant to be **campaign end-game** (or transformation into a new campaign of godly politics). Reaching it is a monumental accomplishment, suitable for the climax of a long-running story where the players perhaps confront the First Flame itself to “break the loop” of creation【8†L126-L134】 or similar world-shaking conclusions.

Progression between these tiers is achieved by a mix of **experience points and narrative milestones**. The game recommends milestone-based advancement (after major story arcs, as reflected in the source material structure【2†L23-L30】), possibly supplemented by XP for smaller achievements. Each tier up requires the character to **overcome a thematic trial** related to that tier’s concept. For example, to go from Flame-Kindled to Triple-Cast, one might have to obtain or craft a *Halo* (a literal artifact or a metaphorical integration of self) that unites the three dice – perhaps by seeking mentors or experiences tied to each Aspect. To become an Axis-Walker, the party likely must physically journey to the Threshold and perform a significant feat there (e.g. close a Hollow breach or align with a Threshold guardian like Solomon). These thematic prerequisites ensure that leveling up is **woven into the story**: players look forward to both the narrative payoff and the mechanical boost.

Mechanically, each new cultivation level grants **broader access to the HALO dice and realms**, plus numerical improvements (higher Aspect caps, more skills, health, etc.) and new special abilities. By design, **early tiers focus on personal abilities**, mid-tiers on **environmental/realm manipulation**, and the top tiers on **cosmic influence and leadership**. This progression scheme delivers the intended *weak-to-strong fantasy*【2†L9-L17】 in a tangible way, taking characters from struggling novices to near-divine powers in a coherent, lore-driven framework.

To summarize, the HALO-based cultivation system ensures that as players progress, **the game experience transforms**: new mechanics come into play that keep the challenge fresh (from simple combat to reality navigation to divine diplomacy), matching the expanding scope of the story. It gives a clear roadmap for growth (satisfying for players who enjoy “leveling up”) while remaining deeply tied to the narrative arcs of the world’s mythology.

## Worship and Divinity Mechanics

Once characters approach the pinnacle of power, the game introduces **divinity mechanics** to handle their interactions with the metaphysical and social aspects of godhood. Even before full apotheosis, characters might start accumulating followers, invoking gods, or tampering with the fabric of faith. The system provides tools for representing **worship, domains, followers, and divine conflict** in gameplay, in a way that is engaging for player characters ascending to godhood or dealing with deities as counterparts.

**Apotheosis Process:** Ascending to godhood is not a trivial flip of a switch; it’s an epic journey and *event* in the narrative. Mechanically, apotheosis is treated as a special **multi-stage quest or ritual**. The character must fulfill specific conditions that align with the cosmology – for example, they might need to **occupy a Throne** (one of the seven cosmological seats of power at the Gyre’s rim) by defeating or usurping its current holder【10†L157-L165】, or perhaps ignite a new “First Flame” fragment within themselves by sacrificing something profound. The Wolfspace research implies that new Throne nodes can be created with immense energy and that the current Thrones took over from predecessors thousands of years ago【10†L169-L172】【10†L139-L148】 – this lore is built into the game’s assumptions: *there is a limited number of divine seats, unless players manage to create another*. Thus, one path to godhood is a campaign climax of **Dethrone and Ascend**: confronting an incumbent god (a major storyline likely) and taking their place. Another path could involve **mantling** – embodying a forgotten deity (for example, if a PC aligns with the erased Mother Goddess Lilith’s essence, they could ascend as the new embodiment of that principle). The rules will outline several possible routes to apotheosis, all of which require **narrative consent** (the GM and group agree it’s the right time) and significant accomplishment.

**Domain and Portfolio:** Upon achieving divinity (or quasi-divinity), a character acquires a **Domain** – a sphere of influence which can be broad (e.g. **Light**, **Chaos**, **Memory**) or more thematic (**Doorways**, **Vengeance**, **Cats**, etc.), usually tied to their character’s story or the manner of ascension. This domain grants them **Divine Traits**: special abilities and rules modifications when acting within that domain. For example, a God of Memory might declare any plot involving forgetting or records to be under their influence, allowing them to alter memory or protect knowledge by divine right. In mechanical terms, these traits can give automatic successes on certain checks, the ability to break specific rules once in a while, or impose **domain effects** on regions (e.g. a fertility deity ensuring nothing dies or everything grows in a blessed area). The domain also dictates what **miracles** the character can perform more easily. We integrate this with the HALO system: each domain resonates with some combination of HALO aspects (e.g. **War** might be Flow+Gate heavy, **Truth** is Mirror+Sight). Rolling those aspects might get advantage or higher effect when used in line with the god’s domain.

**Worship and Followers:** The game quantifies the power of belief via a **Devotion score or Faith points** tied to each deity or ascendant character. Mortals who revere the character contribute to this pool. In gameplay, we handle this similarly to an organization or army that the player “controls”. There is a **follower management subsystem** where players can cultivate and invest in their followers (a bit like a strategy minigame, but kept at narrative level to avoid bookkeeping overwhelm). For example, a newly ascended character might start with a small cult of a few devotees. They can take actions to **spread their creed**, perform public miracles to gain awe, or send prophet NPCs to proselytize. Based on their efforts (and the reactions of the world – e.g. opposing churches or frightened kings might crack down), their **Worship score** goes up or down. A high Worship score can translate to mechanical benefits: perhaps each threshold grants the deity character a **Faith die** they can roll to influence events or a pool of **Prayer points** to spend on miracles. Worship can also act as **currency for divine actions**: want to smite an entire army or create a new star? That might cost a chunk of your accumulated faith energy. In keeping with narrative logic, if the character does things aligned with their believers’ expectations, faith grows; if they act against their professed tenets or suffer humiliating defeat, faith falters (which could even depower them). This system encourages *roleplaying the god* – making choices about how to guide followers, what commandments to issue, and dealing with the consequences. It also provides a built-in check against runaway power: even a Crown-tier character cannot sustain massive reality changes repeatedly if their follower base is small or wavering.

**Relics and Incarnations:** Divine characters may create **holy artifacts** or avatars. The rules will allow a player to invest power into objects or lesser beings. For instance, forging a **Keystone** word or a *Resonance Anchor*【2†L133-L141】 imbued with part of their soul could extend their influence or safeguard against harm (and serve as plot devices – e.g. enemies might seek to steal or corrupt these relics). They can also empower NPC agents (granting a bit of their divinity to a chosen cleric or champion). This effectively lets players act in multiple places or delegate tasks, which is important as their responsibilities widen. Mechanically, creating a relic or incarnation costs some permanent expenditure of power or faith, but yields long-term benefits (like a loyal servant with special abilities, or a magical item the party can use).

**Pantheons and Politics:** The game acknowledges that if one player becomes a god, likely there are other NPC (or PC) deities around – the **cosmic faction dynamics** come to the forefront. The setting includes existing powers like the seven Thrones (divine parasites in the current cosmos)【10†L143-L148】, the *Firstborn* (Lucifer) and possibly the First Flame itself, the Hollow as a quasi-sentient cosmic force, and ancient observers like the Watchers【2†L125-L129】. The divinity mechanics include frameworks for **divine conflict and negotiation**. For example, there may be rules for **Divine Trials**: formal contests or duels between gods that follow agreed constraints (to prevent every clash from destroying reality). There can be **Pantheon Agreements** or laws of heaven that the GM can use to shape high-level play (e.g. a rule that gods cannot directly kill each other without cosmic backlash, forcing them to use mortals as proxies – which creates adventures down on earth). A newly ascended PC might have to either appease or confront the existing pantheon. We’ll provide guidance for staging these encounters in epic, story-rich ways: diplomatic summits at the Crown realm, wars waged through cults and chosen heroes, or metaphysical battles in the Engine where reality’s code is at stake. These scenarios rely on both **role-play and mechanics** – e.g. a debate between two gods might involve each side rolling to rally neutral cosmic entities to their side, using their Worship points as influence currency.

**Realm Creation and Management:** A divine character can shape their own sanctuary. In line with the *Wolfspace* concept of pocket dimensions arising from high quintessence【10†L115-L124】, a god-tier PC can **create a personal realm** if they have enough power. Mechanically this is an extension of the pocket dimension rules: the player defines traits of their realm (size, environment, special rules like “no death occurs here” or “time flows differently”). The more grandiose the realm, the more it costs in faith or permanent power. The realm becomes an extension of the character – a place of safety, but also a target if enemies find a way in. Rules for realm creation ensure it’s balanced: e.g. creating a realm might temporarily weaken the god (spending essence to fuel it), and maintaining it might require a minimum number of believers or a periodic ritual. In turn, having a realm grants strategic advantages: a home base, a place to bring allies, or even trap enemies, and a source of additional quintessence (since the realm likely generates some ambient power the god can tap). 

**Mortal Interaction:** Being a deity doesn’t remove a player from play – rather, it *adds* a new layer. The character still can descend to the mortal world (perhaps via avatars) and adventure with their party, but now the stakes are different. The mechanics reflect this by possibly giving them a **mortal disguise or limiter** (to explain why a god might not just snap fingers to solve everything). For example, a rule like *Incarnation Limits*: when a god walks in Fundament, they operate at a slightly reduced power unless they throw off all constraints (which could cause collateral damage). This keeps challenges interesting and preserves party balance if not all members are gods. 

In summary, the worship and divinity subsystem transforms the game in high tiers into a blend of **strategic leadership and cosmic roleplay**. It provides concrete systems for **worshipper management, realm building, and divine conflict**, so that ascending to godhood opens up new gameplay (managing a cult, influencing civilizations, wrestling with cosmic threats like the Hollow’s nihilism given form【14†L147-L155】) rather than ending the campaign. Yet it remains **grounded in the lore** – everything from *Throne nodes* to the *First Flame* can be directly referenced in these mechanics, making the journey from human to god feel like a continuation of the story’s mythology, not a tacked-on game layer. By handling apotheosis in a structured way, the game ensures players can **pursue ultimate power without breaking the game**, fulfilling the promise of a true weak-to-divine progression fantasy.

## Realms and Cosmological Traversal

The cosmology of *The Unraveling* is a multi-layered reality, and this TTRPG fully embraces that by making planar traversal and exploration a core feature. The setting is built around the **Eight Realms (Biomes)** – concentric (or stacked frequency) layers of reality – each offering unique environments, challenges, and rules of engagement【14†L125-L133】. Understanding and navigating these realms will be crucial for characters as they progress, especially from the mid-tier (Axis-Walker) onward, when inter-realm travel becomes possible.

### The Eight Realms (Biomes) of Reality

The game’s default setting assumes these eight fundamental planes of existence, directly adopted from the series lore:

1. **The Fundament** – *Baseline physical reality.* This is the ordinary world (modern Earth in the novels, or a similar mundane setting in your campaign). Here, physics behave normally and most people are unaware of the higher realms. It’s the densest layer where mortal life thrives【2†L36-L43】【14†L129-L133】. Adventures in the Fundament involve urban fantasy, earthly politics, and the visible effects of supernatural war (e.g. a demon incursion or awakened individuals causing chaos visible to regular people).

2. **The Threshold** – *Realm of space and liminality.* This is often described as *“space between spaces”*, a transitive realm where distance and direction are malleable【2†L41-L44】【14†L129-L133】. Folded space, portals, and the legendary **Roads Between** are features of Threshold. In gameplay, Threshold serves as the gateway to other realms – characters might enter it to fast-travel or to reach pocket dimensions. Movement here can defy normal geometry; one can walk around a corner and end up miles away. A crucial mechanic: travel via Threshold often demands a **toll** or has side effects. As lore states, Solomon’s Roads Between charge *memories as toll*【2†L155-L160】, we incorporate such costs as optional rules – making realm travel a meaningful choice. Encounters in Threshold might involve **Navigators** or space-folding creatures, and dangers like getting lost in infinite doorways. 

3. **The Labyrinth** – *Realm of choice, probability, and branching paths.* Every decision creates echoes here; it’s an ever-shifting maze of **what-ifs**【2†L47-L55】【14†L131-L133】. In the game, the Labyrinth is where fate and chaos are physically manifested. Adventurers entering the Labyrinth might find paths that represent alternate outcomes of their lives, or meet shadow versions of themselves (**Might-Have-Beens** as described in the lore【2†L47-L55】). Mechanically, the Labyrinth can be used for time travel-esque adventures or securing knowledge (“what *would* happen if we do X?” might be answered by exploring a branch in the Labyrinth). However, it’s perilous – one could become lost in possibility or attract the attention of paradoxical entities. We provide a framework for running Labyrinth exploration, including a **branching narrative mechanic**: e.g. mapping choices as dungeon rooms, or using cards to represent doorways labeled with dilemmas. This realm tests players’ problem-solving and decision-making, making it a very *interactive story* environment.

4. **The Reflection** – *Realm of identity and self-perception.* Often described as a **mirror world** where one’s self-image and hidden facets take form【2†L53-L58】【14†L131-L134】. In the game, Reflection is the plane where characters confront their inner demons (sometimes literally). It’s populated by **Reflections** or dopplegangers – aspects of individuals that might act independently. For gameplay, venturing into Reflection could be part of a character’s personal arc (e.g. to heal trauma or reclaim something lost). A GM might run a session where each player’s Reflection appears and challenges them. Mechanics in Reflection might involve inversion of certain stats or opposite outcomes (for example, a brave character’s reflection is cowardly but cunning). Magic that affects the mind or illusions is particularly potent or unpredictable here. A character with unresolved internal conflict may find Reflection extremely dangerous, as the realm *feeds on self-perception*. The rules encourage GMs to use Reflection to deepen characters: perhaps requiring a PC to negotiate or integrate with their mirror-self to leave the realm whole.

5. **The Engine** – *Realm of process, mechanics, and the “code” of reality.* This is the underlying machinery that keeps existence running【2†L61-L68】【14†L133-L136】. The novels portray it as where one might encounter the Architect’s sabotage or see reality’s source code and levers. For the game, The Engine is essentially the **inner workings of magic and physics** – think of it as a cosmic factory floor or a giant clockworks. Adventuring here is like going behind the curtain of the universe: one might alter fundamental laws (with caution!). Mechanically, The Engine might present puzzles that are more technical or logical – for instance, fixing a broken “Script” that governs gravity in a region. Encounters could involve personified algorithms or guardians like the Architect’s minions (rogue programs of reality). The Engine has a steampunk or sci-fi aesthetic in lore (“steampunk-cosmic hybrid”【14†L133-L136】), which the game can emphasize with art and descriptions. In gameplay, damage in the Engine might have side effects (e.g. breaking things in Engine can cause anomalies back in Fundament). It’s a high-level realm, likely not accessed until characters are strong enough to handle its hazards (like self-repairing defenses or raw creative force surges).

6. **The Web** – *Realm of connection, networks, and collective knowledge.* All minds and souls are subtly linked through the Web【2†L67-L74】【14†L133-L136】. This realm is conceptually like a vast network (imagine a psychic internet) where one can trace relationships and communication lines. In-game, the Web is where **telepathy, empathy, and social bonds** become tangible. A skilled character could travel the Web to, say, instantly send a message by riding the connections, or to find information known to someone on the other side of the world. It’s also the realm where collective entities might form (e.g. hive minds or the series’ *Unraveled* predators that “feed on connections”【2†L118-L124】). Mechanics: When entering the Web, the party might navigate a literal web or social graph. Their own relationships become crucial – e.g. a character’s bonds (represented perhaps by **Bond tags** or a relationship map sheet) might determine their “map” in the Web. Encounters could be manifestations of network concepts (like a tangle representing a diplomatic conflict, or a Web-spider that tries to sever connections causing party mistrust). As a realm of connection, cooperation is often rewarded here: PCs sticking together (physically or emotionally) might resist the realm’s attempts to isolate them. Conversely, betrayal or social strife could attract predators.

7. **The Sight** – *Realm of perception and truth.* This is where the **true nature of things** can be seen without filters【2†L73-L80】【14†L135-L137】. It’s hinted that in Sight, the deeper patterns of the Pattern (the cosmic design) are visible. For the game, The Sight realm is basically **absolute revelation** – entering it means confronting reality’s truths and possibly one’s own. Many go mad or transcend when exposed to the Sight. Mechanically, this realm tests a character’s *Insight and willpower*. A GM might treat any visit to Sight as a short, intense experience (as prolonged stay could be campaign-endingly transformative). For instance, a trip into Sight might be how players get a prophecy or discover the real identity of the First Flame, but it could cost them (e.g. temporary blindness or a permanent change of some Aspect due to what they witnessed). We incorporate a mechanic like **Revelation Points**: a character accumulates understanding of cosmic truth while in Sight; if it exceeds a threshold, they might gain an Oracle-like ability (if they endure) or suffer a breakdown. Visually, Sight might be described as a place of blinding light or shifting symbols – possibly each player perceives it differently (the GM could give each a unique description tailored to their character’s perspective). This realm is typically Arc 7 in the story (reserved for near-climax revelations), and similarly in the game it’s likely a late-game realm for the ultimate knowledge before the final confrontation.

8. **The Crown** – *Realm of transcendence and the infinite.* This highest realm is the interface to whatever lies beyond the known Pattern【2†L77-L84】【14†L135-L137】. In the series, the Crown realm is not fully explored until the end, being the summit of the cosmology. In gameplay terms, the Crown is the **endgame plane** – the seat of the First Flame, or the veil before the true Creator, or even the meeting point of all realities (depending on GM interpretation). It’s where mortal understanding fails and only those who have achieved the Crown cultivation (or are otherwise protected) can survive. Adventures in the Crown realm likely revolve around confronting the ultimate antagonist or negotiating with the cosmic source. Mechanically, normal rules can bend in Crown – it might be that in this realm, **the story’s themes dictate outcomes more than any dice**. Perhaps a mechanic: characters of lower tier than Crown automatically get disadvantaged or cannot affect things here unless aided by someone Crown-tier. Alternatively, this is where **toroidal time loops** can be closed – e.g. the final battle might involve actions that echo to the past and future simultaneously【14†L288-L296】. If the campaign goes full metaphysical, players might even step *outside* the story’s reality from here (very meta-narrative). The Crown realm’s inclusion in the game is mainly to have a defined stage for the climax and apotheosis. It provides the backdrop for, say, confronting the First Flame or persuading it to change (remember the notes that perhaps Lilith has to tell God to get therapy【8†L118-L120】 – such a scene would likely occur at the Crown of existence). The game will offer guidance for GMs on running such transcendent scenes, emphasizing narrative resolution and thematic payoff.

**Lost Realms:** The lore also mentions **Four Lost Biomes** that were “devoured by the Hollow”【14†L139-L140】 – originally there were 12 realms. In our design, we keep this as a mysterious element and potential plot device. The lost realms are not accessible by normal means (since they were *consumed*), but the concept of the *Toroidal Timeline*【14†L288-L296】 suggests they might exist on the other side of a cosmic loop or could be restored. For extremely high-level play or future expansions, discovering or reactivating a lost realm could be a campaign goal. We won’t detail them in the core rulebook (preserving the mystique and not overloading new players), but GMs are encouraged to invent what they might have been (e.g. perhaps realms corresponding to aspects like “Dream” or “Desire” that were lost). If players push into Hollow breaches or time paradoxes, you might give them a glimpse of a *Lost Biome* (with heavy Hollow influence, since the Hollow sits where those realms used to be).

### Travel and Exploration Mechanics

Moving between these realms is a hallmark of the game’s exploration pillar. It’s not as simple as casting a teleport spell – each realm has entry requirements or methods, making traversal a mini-game or challenge in itself (but one that *players* can strategize for, fulfilling the intuitive complexity design by turning travel into a meaningful puzzle rather than a hand-wave).

- **Access by Cultivation:** As noted earlier, characters generally gain the ability to enter new realms as they reach certain tiers (e.g. Axis-Walker for basic realm hopping, higher tiers for deeper realms). If a party attempts to go beyond what their strongest member can handle, there may be in-game consequences (they might get repelled or suffer harm). This naturally paces the exposure to the multiverse so as not to overwhelm early play.

- **Paths and Gates:** Many realms have **natural portals** or paths. For example, **Threshold** is reachable via liminal places in the Fundament – a door that appears at midnight in a forgotten alley, or walking the **labyrinth pattern in a churchyard** might phase you to Threshold. We provide tables of plot hooks for such gateways. **Labyrinth** entrances could be found at major crossroads or decisions (the game might even allow entry by paradox – e.g. if a character attempts something that should cause a time paradox, they slip into Labyrinth instead of breaking reality). **Reflection** might open through mirrors or moments of deep self-reflection (perhaps encountering one’s doppelganger in a literal mirror can pull you in). **Engine** access might require complex rituals or going to a high-tech facility that unknowingly interfaces with reality code. **Web** can be entered via a collective ritual or a psychic network (maybe the group all connecting via a dream or a technological mind link). **Sight** might come upon the party unbidden (like a sudden enlightenment event) or via ingestion of a special substance that “opens the third eye.” **Crown** likely only through ascending all the way or via an existing Throne’s domain.

- **Corner Transit and Wolfspace Pockets:** Borrowing from the Wolfspace concept, there exist **hidden routes** that bypass conventional gates. *Corner Transit*【1†L23-L30】 is essentially moving **around** the normal dimensional barriers instead of through them, like walking along the higher-dimensional “corner” to pop out in a different realm. In game terms, a character might attempt a Wolfspace navigation check: success could let them, for instance, go from Fundament to Labyrinth *without crossing Threshold*, by finding a Wolfspace pocket that links to Labyrinth. This is dangerous but offers shortcuts. We’ll include a mechanic like **Wolfspace Navigation** (maybe using advanced math or rare maps as tools) for parties that enjoy exploration. This can be a whole subgame: mapping Wolfspace pockets, dealing with their instability, etc. Wolfspace pockets themselves can be adventure locations – e.g. a smugglers’ hideout “between” realms【1†L41-L49】 or a monster lair that doesn’t fully exist in any one realm. They also offer ways to hide from godly eyes (since “Threshold regions, being between nodes, offer partial concealment” from the Thrones【10†L91-L99】). A clever party might exploit Wolfspace to evade divine surveillance or trap an enemy.

- **Realm Traits:** Each realm imposes certain effects on visitors, which the system will outline so players can prepare. For instance, in **Threshold**, time and distance might be distorted – mechanical effect: navigation is a challenge (the GM might track progress abstractly and use a roll to see if the party stays on course), and there’s a risk of loops (walking in circles literally). In **Labyrinth**, cause and effect may become unpredictable – perhaps every time a choice is made in Labyrinth, a roll is made to determine if a “branch” splits off, potentially manifesting as an encounter. In **Reflection**, one’s **Essence (identity) aspect** might be tested – perhaps characters must periodically make a save using their Essence to avoid having their roles swapped with their reflection. **Engine** might suppress or enhance certain powers (e.g. magic might require logic puzzles to execute). **Web** could enforce empathy – e.g. if one party member feels pain, all do, unless they isolate themselves. **Sight** might strip away illusions automatically – good for seeing truth, bad if you rely on any buff that is essentially a self-deception. **Crown** might simply be overwhelming, requiring constant expenditure of willpower to stay present.

- **Cosmic Cartography:** Because planar travel can be complex, the game will encourage parties to engage with experts or tools. There might be NPC **Cartographers of the Liminal** (like the Institute for Liminal Cartography hinted by the Wolfspace paper’s author affiliation【1†L5-L12】). These NPCs can guide or give missions. The players might find a **Realm Map** artifact which gives hints (like showing known gates or safe routes). Additionally, the campaign setting will have **hub locations**: for example, an outpost at the Threshold where various realm-walkers meet to trade information (think of it as a planar tavern). Through such hubs, GMs can let the party gather rumors (“The Reflection can be entered during an eclipse at the mirror lake”) and make realm traversal more of a quest and less of a guessing game.

- **Vehicles and Vessels:** For flavor and practicality, the game might include conveyances for realm travel. Perhaps there are **subway trains that run through the Web** or **ships that sail the Quintessence currents between realms**. One could even ride a tamed Hollow manifestation through the Gnaw to reach a lost realm (very dangerous!). This gives the opportunity for some fantastical travel scenes (imagine flying through the Engine’s clockwork on a steampunk airship, or taking an elevator that moves upward from city to city and eventually into the sky to Threshold). Mechanically, vehicles provide protection and ease some travel rolls, but might attract threats or require special fuel (like memories, or literal starlight, depending on the realm).

**Cosmic Factions and Travel:** As part of traversal, the **factions** from lore will play a role. For example, **The Concordat** or Coalition operates across realms via their intelligence network【2†L93-L102】 – PCs allied with them might get easier access to travel (they maintain secret portals or safehouses). **The Hollow’s forces** often tear holes between realms to invade【2†L109-L117】 – these can be events the party encounters (like a realm bleed where Hollow energy seeps from the Gnaw in Threshold into Fundament). **The Watchers** are neutral but might intervene if players try something extreme like destabilizing realms; they could appear in travel sequences to issue cryptic warnings【2†L125-L129】. The travel mechanics thus tie into faction dynamics: who controls the gates? Are there tolls or blockades set by certain groups? The game can include scenarios like *The Siege of Threshold Road* where an faction tries to monopolize realm access and the players must negotiate or break through.

In conclusion, the Realms and Traversal system ensures that the **cosmology is a playground** for exploration. It provides diverse settings to adventure in (from gritty city streets to abstract planes) and makes *getting there* an adventure in itself. By using lore-consistent methods (fold-walking, corner transit, realm-specific entry rituals)【1†L23-L30】【2†L155-L160】, it reinforces the feeling that players are moving through a living, breathing multiverse with its own physics and politics. This fulfills the design goal of integrating core lore (the Threshold/Wolfspace ideas, cosmic layer structure) into actual gameplay and supports emergent gameplay – clever players will surely find unexpected ways to use realm-hopping to their advantage, yielding memorable moments that feel *earned* because the rules empowered their creativity rather than simply teleporting by GM fiat.

## Narrative Infrastructure and Roleplay Support

Beyond mechanics and lore, the Unraveling TTRPG provides a framework to support **rich roleplaying, character-driven storytelling, and collaborative narrative creation**. The goal is to make sure the game’s heavy themes and epic scope remain *personal and engaging* at the table. Several features and subsystems are built in to encourage and guide narrative development:

**Character Backstory and Arc Integration:** During character creation, players are prompted to tie their characters into the world’s mythos and factions. The system uses **Background Anchors** – similar to aspects in Fate or background bonds in D&D, but tailored to this setting. Examples might include *“Child of the Hollow War”*, *“Haunted by a Past Life (First Flame fragment)”*, or *“Former Coalition Operative”*. Each Anchor provides not just flavor but a small mechanical perk *and* a built-in story thread. GMs are encouraged (with XP incentives) to weave these threads into the campaign. For instance, if a PC has *“Destined for a Throne”* as an anchor, the GM might introduce prophetic dreams or a rival claimant as part of that character’s arc. The arc-based structure of the source material (each arc focusing on mastering a realm or confronting a personal demon) is mirrored in game pacing – we suggest campaigns be organized into **Arcs or Milestones** that center on one character’s development at a time (rotating spotlight), so every character gets their *“Lily moment”* of growth. This is supported by a **Milestone XP system**: achieving personal story milestones grants bonus experience or immediate Aspect advancements, rewarding players for engaging with their narrative.

**Dramatic Beats and Emotional Resonance:** The tone of the source is a blend of cosmic horror, humor, and heartfelt emotion. To capture this, the game introduces the concept of **Dramatic Beats**. These are essentially flags players or GMs can raise when a scene is entering a crucial emotional territory (a confrontation with a father figure, a lover’s farewell before a battle, a crisis of faith in the face of the Hollow’s despair). When a Dramatic Beat is triggered, certain mechanics shift to second priority and narrative outcomes take precedence. For example, in a Beat, a player might automatically succeed or dramatically fail at a crucial roll – whichever would make the story more powerful – with the group’s consent, possibly at the cost of a future complication (this is somewhat akin to Powered by the Apocalypse’s concept of *making a hard move* or *succeeding at a cost*). The game actually encourages players to propose such moments: “I want to trigger a Beat: my character drops their weapon and tries to talk the enraged angel down.” If everyone’s on board, mechanics might bend (the angel might be swayed without a roll because it’s fitting, or maybe that triggers a social conflict resolution where stakes are higher than usual). We also include safety and consent tools here (Session Zero guidelines, X-card, etc.) since touching on deep emotions requires trust and calibration.

**HALO Oracle for Storytelling:** In addition to resolving powers, the **HALO dice oracle** is available as a **storytelling aid** for players and GMs. Stuck on what happens next in a mystery? Draw a HALO spread: the Axis/Vector/Archetype tables can generate a prompt (e.g. *Mind & Narrative + Illuminate + The Tower* might suggest a revelation that upends what the characters know【6†L39-L47】【6†L49-L57】). We provide a simplified oracle table in the GM section specifically for improvisation: one roll might give an event, twist, or a thematic element to introduce. This encourages a **collaborative storytelling approach** where even the game system can “GM” a bit, surprising players and GM alike with emergent plot points. It’s particularly useful for solo play or GM-less scenes (the product snapshot of HALO even envisioned solo and co-op play【6†L4-L8】, and we carry that spirit here). Players can also use the oracle for personal decisions: e.g. if a player is unsure how their character feels about something, they could roll the Archetype die – a result of *The Hermit* might indicate their character withdraws introspectively, whereas *The Sun* might indicate they respond with clarity and optimism.

**Dialogue and Voice:** The source writing has a very distinct voice – witty, irreverent, and profound. To help GMs and players capture that vibe, the game includes plentiful **examples of dialogue and tone** in sidebars. Small vignettes of in-character exchanges (for example, a snarky banter between a PC and an NPC god, reflecting the *“sacred irreverence”* the author notes champion【14†L187-L195】) illustrate how to mix humor and gravitas. We explicitly encourage players to let their characters express themselves with that mix of **profane and sacred** if it fits – e.g. a table rule might be “one well-timed F-bomb that fits character or situation can grant a +1 bonus or restore an Aegis token,” echoing how the novel finds power in *sacred profanity*. Similarly, moments of vulnerability and intimacy are supported – the lore’s emphasis on sexuality as sacred and not shyed away from【14†L269-L277】 is noted as a thematic element; while the game doesn’t force this content, it lets groups know that exploring characters’ desires or romantic arcs is on-theme and can be tied to mechanics (perhaps a **Bond** mechanic where deepening a relationship can provide mechanical support in key moments, analogous to how love or camaraderie can literally empower characters against the Hollow’s loneliness). These touches help maintain thematic alignment with the source’s voice.

**Faction Play and Politics:** On a larger scale, narrative infrastructure includes tools for managing **faction-based storytelling**. Given the cosmic faction dynamics (Coalition vs Hollow cults vs Watchers etc.), we provide a **Faction Meter or Influence chart**: a way to track how major factions view the party and how the factions themselves are faring. If the party heavily aids the Coalition’s cause, for example, their **Concordat Reputation** might increase, yielding them resources or information【2†L93-L102】. Conversely, if they often tap into Hollow powers or use violence wantonly, **Hollow corruption** might tick up, triggering more Hollow encounters or even personal consequences (like a creeping nihilism they must resist). This is akin to a “fronts” system where the GM can move faction plans forward on a timeline – e.g. *Manifestation Nodes* of the Hollow spreading【2†L109-L117】 as time goes on, unless thwarted. Players can engage these via quests (maybe they choose to focus this arc on shutting down a Manifestation Node in a city). By making faction influence a trackable element, the game enables strategic roleplay: players might hold a council with allies to decide which cosmic threat to handle next, essentially co-authoring the campaign’s direction. It also means the narrative responds to their actions on a grand scale, showing tangible impact beyond individual encounters.

**Personal Horror and Support:** The Unraveling deals with heavy themes like mental health (Lily’s PTSD, neurodivergence, bipolar, etc. are acknowledged in the text【2†L165-L173】). The RPG includes an option for reflecting this through a **Stress or Humanity mechanic** (inspired by systems like *Call of Cthulhu* sanity or *Vampire* humanity, but tailored to themes of loneliness vs connection). For example, exposure to the Hollow’s influence – essentially cosmic loneliness and depression【14†L149-L157】 – can inflict **Despair points**. If a character accumulates too many Despair points without relief, they risk manifestations of inner darkness (perhaps their Reflection might act out, or they suffer a breakdown). To counter this, the game encourages roleplay of coping mechanisms and mutual support: characters can perform **Connection scenes** (heart-to-heart talks, recalling meaningful memories, grounding rituals) to remove Despair points or gain **Hope** buffs. This mechanic not only reinforces the narrative theme that connection and purpose fend off the Hollow, but also incentivizes players to actually engage in those quieter roleplay moments that deepen characterization. It must be emphasized with appropriate safety tools (since players might draw on real feelings), but when done well, it produces some of the most memorable sessions – the kind where characters bond and the eventual triumph over darkness feels earned.

**Flexibility in Tone:** Finally, the narrative framework is adjustable for tone. While the default assumption blends dark fantasy with gallows humor (again, *Solo Leveling’s power fantasy meets Discworld satire*【2†L9-L17】), groups may lean more on one or the other. We provide “tone dials” suggestions: e.g. for a **more earnest epic** you might downplay the fourth-wall humor and play the gods completely straight; for a **gonzo comedic campaign**, you let the absurdity flow (maybe incorporating meta-commentary like the characters slight awareness of being in a story, which the Unraveling arcs hint at with meta-awareness increasing). The narrative tools (like Dramatic Beats, HALO oracle) work in either case, it’s just a matter of how they’re described. By acknowledging this, we ensure the dev team (and eventual GMs) know that the **voice of the game can be tuned** without breaking the underlying structure.

In sum, the Narrative Infrastructure of the game is about **empowering the players and GM to tell a story with the same heart as the novels**. It’s not just a combat simulator or a lore dump – it actively guides the table toward the kinds of scenes and arcs that define *The Unraveling*: personal growth amid cosmic chaos, the triumph of connection over despair, irreverent wit in the face of horror, and always, **characters who feel real** even as they become mythic. The mechanics and prompts provided serve as scaffolding to make improvised storytelling easier, helping the group maintain pacing and thematic focus. By prioritizing narrative support at the mechanical level, we fulfill the aim of **narrative-driven play** and ensure the game delivers not just excitement, but also meaning and emotional resonance.

## Modularity and Extensibility

One of the key design goals is to build a system that can **grow and adapt** beyond the initial core setting, without losing its balance or coherence. To that end, the Unraveling TTRPG is architected with modularity in mind. Here we outline how the game’s components can be extended or customized, and how third-party or homebrew content can be supported.

**Layered Rule Design:** The rules are structured in **layers** – a stable core and optional modules on top. The **Core Layer** includes universal mechanics: the Aspect system, HALO dice resolution, basic combat and conflict rules, and the baseline human tier gameplay. This layer is setting-agnostic in many respects (one could theoretically use the core system to run a non-Unraveling game by ignoring the lore-specific terms). On top of that, we have **Cosmic Layer** rules (realms, cultivation tiers, divinity, etc.) which are tied to the Unraveling universe assumptions. However, each “cosmic” feature is self-contained: for example, the *Realms* travel rules can be turned off or replaced if a setting doesn’t involve planar travel, without breaking core play. We achieve this by ensuring that core play (say an adventure set entirely in Fundament with street-level characters) can function with just Core Layer rules. Everything else is additive. The **Expansion Layer** is where future content packs plug in – these could be official expansions or fan-made. Each expansion will declare what it modifies or adds (much like a D&D module might say “this adds new classes and a new region”). Clear guidelines will be provided on how to design content that fits within the point budgets and narrative scope of each tier.

**Custom Realms and Settings:** The framework allows for **alternate cosmologies** by treating the Eight Realms as a template rather than a hard requirement. A module could introduce a wholly new set of realms (for instance, an alternate dimension or a sci-fi parallel). To support this, the travel system uses a generic interface: realms are defined by a set of properties (entry method, governing Aspect, primary challenges, etc.). As long as a new realm or plane is defined in those terms, it can slot in. For example, if someone wanted to create a Norse mythology module, they could map the Nine Realms of Yggdrasil to the mechanics (some might correspond to the existing ones; others could be new but follow similar patterns). The **HALO system is similarly extensible**: the default set of dice faces and meanings is provided, but the “engine is table-agnostic” approach【17†L36-L43】 means you could re-skin the dice with new terminology to fit a different mythos while keeping the mechanical structure. We’ll include an example: say a cyberpunk expansion might redefine Flow/Mirror/Gate in technological terms (Hardware, Software, Network, perhaps) with corresponding lists of 8 effects each – the core rolling and combo mechanics remain identical, so balance is maintained.

**Balanced Expansion of Powers:** To ensure new content doesn’t break the game, we impose a **balance framework**. Every ability or enemy or item is given a **Power Rank** keyed to the cultivation tiers. Content for Spark/Flame level is Rank 1, going up to Rank 7 for Crown-level. We’ll advise expansion designers that any new power must fit the scope of its rank. For instance, a new spell introduced in an expansion for Rank 3 (Triple-Cast level) should be roughly equivalent in impact to other Rank 3 abilities in core (like it might let a character temporarily influence one realm or do a powerful attack, but not permanently alter a realm – that would be Rank 5+ territory). The core book will have a section, likely in an Appendix, giving **design guidelines and benchmarks**: e.g. at Rank 2 a single character can defeat a squad of normal soldiers or solve a city-scale problem; at Rank 5 they can tackle an army or solve a country-scale problem, etc. This provides a measuring stick to keep contributions in line. Additionally, we encourage a playtest and community feedback loop for third-party content – possibly an online repository or forum where homebrew can be discussed and balanced collaboratively.

**Alternate Play Modes:** Modularity also extends to **play modes**. The game can be played as a long-form campaign, but we also outline modes for **one-shots** or **short arcs**, with simplified rules. For example, we might include a “Cinematic Mode” as a module where instead of granular Aspect points and skills, you use a trimmed-down narrative stat block, suitable for convention games or quick-play. There’s also potential for a **solo mode or GM-less co-op mode** (given the oracle origins). An official module or appendix might show how to use the HALO Decision Engine mechanics【6†L4-L8】【6†L111-L120】 in a solo RPG context, letting a single player experience the story by drawing cards or dice for prompts and using the core rules to resolve key moments. These modes are clearly separated from core rules so as not to confuse primary gameplay, but having them available increases the game’s flexibility and audience reach (someone might buy the TTRPG just to play solo narrative oracle adventures, effectively using it as a sandbox storytelling kit – which is possible due to the HALO oracle inclusion).

**Third-Party Licensing and Tools:** While not a mechanic per se, from a design plan perspective it’s worth noting that we intend to support third-party content via a license (in the vein of popular RPG licenses) so that creators can legally publish their own realms, campaigns, and expansions. To make their lives easier, we will release a **System Reference Document (SRD)** that details the core mechanics without lore, and a **Lore Companion Document** summarizing the world elements open for use. This separation means someone could take the core engine and do something completely different (which is fine), or integrate with the lore if they want to create, say, “The Unraveling: Asian Mythology” expansion or a fan module exploring one of the Lost Biomes. We’ll also encourage digital tool development: the straightforward nature of HALO dice and tables means they could be integrated into virtual tabletops or character builders. Our design will thus produce data and formulas that are easy to code (e.g. a formula for HALO dice combination outcomes). Perhaps the Collab team’s experience with the **HALO Pocket Labyrinth** app and oracle could feed into official digital support, like a companion app for rolling the HALO dice or tracking quintessence (the README of the repo hints at online and multiplayer features【12†L1-L9】【12†L16-L23】, showing the team’s capability in that area). A modular digital approach (where a GM can toggle on the divinity module or off, etc.) would mirror the tabletop design.

**Future-Proofing Setting Changes:** The Unraveling story itself evolves (the arcs indicate changes in the world like web awakening, etc.). If future novels or lore updates introduce new revelations (say a 9th realm, or a change in the nature of the Hollow), the TTRPG can accommodate those as new modules or errata rather than requiring an overhaul. For example, if it’s revealed that the Hollow actually has a personified avatar that could become a playable power source, we can add a “Hollow Pact” module with rules for characters channeling the Hollow (perhaps similar to warlock patrons in other games). The core remains the same, just extended. We are essentially **mirroring the open-ended, evolving nature of the narrative** in the game design: the system can **unravel and re-weave itself** in bits without falling apart.

**Community Content Integration:** The design also considers community-driven additions like **fan realms or scenarios**. We might create an official repository or magazine that features top-rated homebrew content, effectively playtested and curated. This not only extends the game’s life but also allows fans of the series to see their imaginative contributions become part of the wider universe. Given the series’ themes of collaboration (the Coalition networks, shared consciousness in Web, etc.), it’s fitting that the game encourages a collaborative approach to world-building. The modular architecture ensures that a cool idea someone has (e.g. a new faction or a new magic subsystem) can often be slotted in as an optional rule without needing to tear down anything else.

In summary, modularity and extensibility are baked into the DNA of this TTRPG. The system is **robust but flexible**, with clearly defined points where new content can attach. By maintaining balance guidelines and providing support for expansion creators, we aim to cultivate an ecosystem where the game continues to thrive and evolve, much like the living story world it’s based on. Whether a group wants to strictly follow the canon or take the mechanics on a wild remix, the game will accommodate them, making it a platform for imagination rooted in the beloved lore.
